claim: Inferior temporal (IT) cortex is thought to most directly underlie core visual object recognition in human and non-human primates.
source: Among visual areas, the inferior temporal (IT) cortex is thought to most directly underlie core visual object recognition in human and non-human primates (Ito et al., 1995; Rajalingham and DiCarlo, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ito et al., 1995; Rajalingham and DiCarlo, 2019)

claim: Simple weighted sums of IT neuronal population activity can accurately explain and predict human and monkey core object recognition performance over dozens of tasks.
source: For example, simple weighted sums of IT neuronal population activity can accurately explain and predict human and monkey core object recognition (COR) performance over dozens of such tasks (Majaj et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Majaj et al., 2015)

claim: Direct suppression of IT activity disrupts core object recognition behavior.
source: Moreover, direct suppression of IT activity disrupts COR behavior (Afraz et al., 2015; Rajalingham and DiCarlo, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Afraz et al., 2015; Rajalingham and DiCarlo, 2019)

claim: Many individual IT neurons show high tolerance to object latent variables including size, position, and pose.
source: These results were found in the face of significant variation in object latent variables including size, position, and pose, and the high performance of the simple IT readout (weighted sum) rests on the fact that many individual IT neurons show high tolerance to those variables (DiCarlo et al., 2012; Hung et al., 2005; Li et al., 2009), reviewed by DiCarlo et al., 2012.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (DiCarlo et al., 2012; Hung et al., 2005; Li et al., 2009)

claim: Simulated IT 'neurons' in the deep layers of artificial neural networks have tolerance and provide accurate approximations of the adult ventral visual stream processing.
source: Simulated IT 'neurons' in the deep layers of artificial neural networks (ANNs) have such tolerance and provide quite accurate approximations of the adult ventral visual stream processing (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Rajalingham et al., 2018; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Rajalingham et al., 2018; Yamins et al., 2014)

claim: ANNs are produced by training with millions of supervised (labeled) training images, an experience regime that is almost surely not biologically plausible over evolution or postnatal development.
source: However, those ANNs are produced by training with millions of supervised (labeled) training images, an experience regime that is almost surely not biologically plausible over evolution or postnatal development.
evidence: Based on inference about biological plausibility of training regimes

claim: The temporal stability of object identity under natural viewing has been proposed as a key available source of unsupervised information that might be leveraged by the visual system to construct neural tolerance.
source: The temporal stability of object identity under natural viewing (i.e., objects do not rapidly jump in and out of existence) has been proposed as a key available source of unsupervised information that might be leveraged by the visual system to construct neural tolerance, even during adulthood (Földiák, 1991; Hénaff et al., 2019; Rolls and Stringer, 2006; Wallis et al., 2009; Wallis et al., 2009; Wiskott and Sejnowski, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical work (Földiák, 1991; Hénaff et al., 2019; Rolls and Stringer, 2006; Wallis et al., 2009; Wallis et al., 2009; Wiskott and Sejnowski, 2002)

claim: Unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience reshapes position tolerance in humans as measured at the behavioral level.
source: Consistent with this view, psychophysical results from human subjects show that unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience (i.e., laboratory situations in which object do jump in and out of existence) reshapes position tolerance (Cox et al., 2005), pose tolerance (Wallis and Bülthoff, 2001), and depth illumination tolerance (Wallis et al., 2009) as measured at the behavioral level.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Cox et al., 2005)

claim: Unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience reshapes pose tolerance in humans as measured at the behavioral level.
source: Consistent with this view, psychophysical results from human subjects show that unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience (i.e., laboratory situations in which object do jump in and out of existence) reshapes position tolerance (Cox et al., 2005), pose tolerance (Wallis and Bülthoff, 2001), and depth illumination tolerance (Wallis et al., 2009) as measured at the behavioral level.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Wallis and Bülthoff, 2001)

claim: Unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience reshapes depth illumination tolerance in humans as measured at the behavioral level.
source: Consistent with this view, psychophysical results from human subjects show that unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience (i.e., laboratory situations in which object do jump in and out of existence) reshapes position tolerance (Cox et al., 2005), pose tolerance (Wallis and Bülthoff, 2001), and depth illumination tolerance (Wallis et al., 2009) as measured at the behavioral level.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Wallis et al., 2009)

claim: Unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience reshapes IT neuronal position and size tolerance in adult macaque IT.
source: Similarly, neurophysiological data from adult macaque IT show that unsupervised exposure to unnatural temporal contiguity experience reshapes IT neuronal position and size tolerance (Li et al., 2009; Li and DiCarlo, 2008; Li and DiCarlo, 2010), in a manner that is qualitatively consistent with the human behavioral data.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Li et al., 2009; Li and DiCarlo, 2008; Li and DiCarlo, 2010)

claim: The overall model largely predicted the mean direction, magnitude, and time course of human performance changes after being constrained by neurophysiological data.
source: We found that our model, after constrained by neurophysiological data, largely predicted the mean direction, magnitude, and time course of human performance changes.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and model predictions presented in the study (Figures 2 and 5)

claim: There is a previously unreported dependency of the observed human performance change on the initial task difficulty.
source: We also found a previously unreported dependency of the observed human performance change on the initial task difficulty.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: A total of 174 human subjects on Amazon Mechanical Turk participated in the main experiment.
source: A total of 174 human subjects on Amazon Mechanical Turk (see Materials and methods and Kar et al., 2019; Majaj et al., 2015; Rajalingham et al., 2018) participated in this experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: In experiment u1 (swapped exposure events), discrimination of the target face pair viewed at big size decreased with increasing numbers of exposure events.
source: In experiment u1 (swapped exposure events), we found that discrimination of the target face pair viewed at big size decreased with increasing numbers of exposure events (Figure 2A; top rows; red solid line; n = 102 subjects).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In experiment u1, there was little to no change in the performance for the non-exposed (small size) versions of the target faces.
source: We found little to no change in the performance for the non-exposed (small size) versions of those same faces (black dashed line; mean initial d´ is 1.2 ± 0.1) or for non-exposed control faces (also tested at big size, black solid line).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In experiment u2 (non-swapped exposure events), discrimination of the target face pair viewed at big size increased with increasing numbers of exposure events.
source: In experiment u2 (non-swapped exposure events), we found that discrimination of the target face pair viewed at big size increased with increasing numbers of exposure events (Figure 2B; top rows; blue solid line; n = 36 subjects).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: After ~800 exposure events, the exposure-induced learning effects appeared to plateau in both 'breaking' tolerance conditions (experiment u1) and 'building' tolerance conditions (experiment u2).
source: Interestingly, after ~800 exposure events, the exposure-induced learning effects appeared to plateau in both 'breaking' tolerance conditions (experiment u1, Figure 2A) and 'building' tolerance conditions (experiment u2, Figure 2B), suggesting a limit in the measurable behavioral effects (see Discussion).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B

claim: In experiment u3, size tolerance first increased with non-swapped ('build') exposures and then decreased with swapped ('break') exposures.
source: Consistent with the results of experiments u1 and u2, we found that size tolerance first increased with non-swapped ('build') exposures and then decreased with swapped ('break') exposures (Figure 2C), and that the effect did not spill over to the control objects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The generative IT model captures the IT neuronal representation space with a multi-dimensional Gaussian (MDG) model.
source: This generative IT model captures the IT neuronal representation space with a multi-dimensional Gaussian (MDG) model, assuming the distribution of IT population responses is Gaussian-like for each object (see Materials and methods for Gaussian validation) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by model description and validation in Figure 3A

claim: 81.25% (52 out of 64 distributions for 64 objects) of the IT population response distributions were Gaussian.
source: We tested this hypothesis with a normality test and found that 81.25% (52 out of 64 distributions for 64 objects) of the IT population response distributions were Gaussian (reject when p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical test on IT population data

claim: The simulated IT population responses were highly correlated with the actual IT neural data (r = 0.93 ± 0.01).
source: One typical example of that is shown in Figure 3C, revealing high correlation of the two RSMs (r = 0.93 ± 0.01).
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 3C

claim: The number of simulated IT sites required to match human performance was similar across different tasks (260 ± 23 IT sites given 20 training images).
source: Consistent with Majaj et al., 2015, we found that the number of simulated IT sites required to match human was similar across different tasks (260 ± 23) IT sites given 20 training images (tested over 24 object discrimination tasks: low variation eight-way tests: eight basic level, eight car identification, and eight face identification tasks; previously used in Majaj et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by model fitting to human performance data across 24 tasks

claim: The match between the decoded simulated IT performance and human performance over all discrimination tasks was r = 0.83 ± 0.05.
source: Specifically, we here used 260 sites with 20 training samples for all tasks, and the match between the decoded simulated IT performance and human performance over all discrimination tasks was r = 0.83 ± 0.05 (n = 24 tasks), similar to previously reported match between decoded neural IT performance and human for the same tasks (r = 0.868 from Majaj et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by model performance comparison to human data

claim: The unsupervised IT plasticity rule states that the modification of firing rate of the leading image is equal to the difference of firing rate between lagging and leading images multiplied by a plasticity rate α.
source: Our plasticity rule states that the modification of FR of each IT unit to the leading image at time t is equal to the difference of FR between lagging and leading images multiplied by a plasticity rate α.
evidence: Direct statement of the plasticity rule equation

claim: The best plasticity rate α is 0.0016 nru per exposure event.
source: The best α is 0.0016 nru per exposure event (nru = normalized response units; see Materials and methods for intuition about approximate spike rate changes).
evidence: Supported by fitting to prior monkey IT neurophysiology data (Li and DiCarlo, 2010)

claim: The overall model did a very good job of predicting the direction, magnitude, and time course of the changes in human behavior for each of the three unsupervised experiments.
source: For each experiment, we found that the overall model did a very good job of predicting the direction, magnitude, and time course of the changes in human behavior.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions to experimental data in Figure 5

claim: Model variants with IT plasticity rate either four times smaller or four times bigger than empirically observed produced predictions clearly different in magnitude than the observations.
source: In both cases, the predictions of these (non-biology-matched) model variants were now clearly different in magnitude than the observations (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by model sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: For initially easy tasks (d' > ~2.5) and initially difficult tasks (d' < ~0.5), smaller learning effects were observed than tasks with intermediate initial performance.
source: In particular, for initially easy tasks (d' > ~2.5) and initially difficult tasks (d' < ~0.5), we observed a smaller learning effect than tasks with intermediate initial performance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The average performance tended to plateau around 90%, which is taken as an indication of a performance ceiling attributed to lapses.
source: We found that the average performance tended to plateau around 90%, which we take as an indication of a performance ceiling that cannot be explained by a lack of sensory evidence, and thus we attribute to multiple types of downstream errors collectively referred to as lapses.
evidence: Supported by analysis of human performance data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: The distribution of task performance accuracy for basic-level tasks has a maximum of 95.0%.
source: We also directly quantified the distribution of task performance accuracy for basic-level tasks (easy tasks: d' > 2.5) in our experiments (Figure 6) and found that the distribution has a maximum of 95.0% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: The lapse rate of the subject pool is ~10%.
source: These analyses suggest that the lapse rate of our subject pool is ~10% (i.e., 95% accuracy for two choice tasks with perfect sensory evidence), which is consistent with prior work on human lapse rates (<20%; Manning et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by analysis of human performance data and citation to prior work (Manning et al., 2018)

claim: The overall model with 9% or 20% lapse rate reasonably explained the dependence of the observed magnitude of human d' changes as a function of initial human d'.
source: We simulated the effect of 9% lapse rate and 20% lapse rate (i.e., we told the model to make random guesses on 9% or 20% of trials, regardless of the strength of sensory evidence) and found that these new overall models reasonably explained the dependence of the observed magnitude of human d' changes as a function of initial human d' (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by model predictions with lapse rate shown in Figure 6B

claim: The accuracy of the model predictions supports the hypothesis that temporally contiguous unsupervised learning could help shape neural representations that underlie robust core object recognition, even in adults.
source: More broadly, the accuracy of the model predictions supports the overarching hypothesis that temporally contiguous unsupervised learning could help shape neural representations that underlie robust (i.e., tolerant) COR, even in adults.
evidence: Based on inference from the overall results of the study

claim: The overall model implicitly assumes that monkey IT and human IT are approximately identical.
source: This was surprising because the overall model implicitly assumes that monkey IT and human IT are approximately identical (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Rajalingham et al., 2018), the linkage of IT to COR behavior is approximately identical in monkeys and humans (as previously suggested; Majaj et al., 2015), human unsupervised IT plasticity is the same as monkey IT plasticity, and that little or no behaviorally relevant plastic changes occur in the mechanistic linkage between IT and behavior during or after unsupervised visual experience (at least not at the time scales of these experiments: 1.5–2 hr).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Rajalingham et al., 2018) and inference about model assumptions

claim: The overall model could predict behavioral learning effects in the low initial d' and moderate initial d' regime for different exposure types, even though the images used in those tasks are in a different d' regime from the specific images used in the neuronal plasticity experiments.
source: We think it is quite interesting and demonstrative of this approach that the overall model could predict behavioral learning effects in the low initial d' and moderate initial d' regime for different exposure types (build or break), even though the images used in those tasks are in a different d' regime from the specific images used in the neuronal plasticity experiments used to tune the model learning (i.e., those neural experiments were done with images in a high d' regime).
evidence: Based on inference from model predictions and experimental design

claim: The most likely possibility for the discrepancy between model predictions and human learning data at the longest exposure durations is that learning over long periods involves more complicated neural mechanisms than those captured by the simplified unsupervised IT plasticity rule.
source: The most likely possibility is that learning over long periods of unsupervised exposure involves more complicated neural mechanisms than those that are captured by our simplified unsupervised IT plasticity rule.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about model limitations

claim: The existence of lapse rate imposes a ceiling on measured performance.
source: Our simulation, and previous studies, suggests that the existence of lapse rate imposes a ceiling on measured performance (Gold and Ding, 2013; Pisupati et al., 2021; Prins, 2012; Wichmann and Hill, 2001) and thus would strongly mask measured performance changes in that (high d') regime.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Gold and Ding, 2013; Pisupati et al., 2021; Prins, 2012; Wichmann and Hill, 2001) and model simulations

claim: Földiák suggested that the internal representation should mimic physical entities in real life, which are subject to continuous changes in time.
source: Földiák suggested that the internal representation should mimic physical entities in real life, which are subject to continuous changes in time (Földiák, 1990; Földiák, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical work (Földiák, 1990; Földiák, 1991)

claim: Wallis and Bulthoff found that unsupervised exposure to temporal image sequences of different views of different faces led to performance deficits compared to sequences of the same face.
source: Wallis and Bulthoff found that unsupervised exposure to temporal image sequences of different views of different faces led to performance deficits compared to sequences of the same face (Wallis and Bülthoff, 2001; Wallis and Bülthoff, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Wallis and Bülthoff, 2001; Wallis and Bülthoff, 1999)

claim: Cox et al. showed that 'swapped' unsupervised experience of pairs of images across saccades could reduce ('break') position tolerance of object discrimination.
source: Cox et al. showed that 'swapped' unsupervised experience of pairs of images across saccades could reduce ('break') position tolerance of object discrimination (Cox et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Cox et al., 2005)

claim: Balas and Sinha showed that observing object motion can increase both generalization to nearby views and selectivity to exposed views.
source: Balas and Sinha showed that observing object motion can increase both generalization to nearby views and selectivity to exposed views (Balas and Sinha, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Balas and Sinha, 2008)

claim: Li and DiCarlo found that, over ~1.5 hr of unsupervised exposure of 'swapped' temporal statistics, the size and position tolerance of IT neuronal responses were significantly modified, and that these changes were not reward or task dependent.
source: Li and DiCarlo directly tested the role of unsupervised visual experience in IT neuronal tolerance by manipulating the identities and properties of objects presented consecutively in time (Li and DiCarlo, 2008; Li and DiCarlo, 2010). They found that, over ~1.5 hr of unsupervised exposure of 'swapped' temporal statistics, the size and position tolerance of IT neuronal responses were significantly modified, and that these changes were not reward or task dependent (Li and Dicarlo, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Li and DiCarlo, 2008; Li and DiCarlo, 2010; Li and Dicarlo, 2012)

claim: Qualitatively similar temporal continuity-dependent neuronal plasticity has been observed in rodents during development.
source: Qualitatively similar temporal continuity-dependent neuronal plasticity has also been observed in rodents during development (Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020)

claim: The results of this study show that behavioral effects can be largely accounted for by the IT neural effects.
source: Although prior experimental work seemed qualitatively consistent with the overarching theoretical idea, it did not demonstrate that the behavioral learning effects could be explained by the IT neural effects. The results of our study here show that those two effects are quantitatively consistent with each other – the behavioral effects can be largely accounted for by the IT neural effects.
evidence: Based on inference from the overall results of the study

claim: Okamura et al. showed that continuous motion or view presentation is not necessary to form tolerance, rather, enough exposure to different views (even in random sequence) can support view-invariant object recognition.
source: Okamura et al. showed that continuous motion or view presentation is not necessary to form tolerance, rather, enough exposure to different views (even in random sequence) can support view-invariant object recognition (Okamura et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Okamura et al., 2014)

claim: Van Meel and Op de Beeck investigated whether temporal continuity experience can alter size-tolerance representation in human LOC using fMRI and reported no observable effects.
source: Van Meel and Op de Beeck investigated whether temporal continuity experience can alter size-tolerance representation in human LOC using fMRI and reported no observable effects (Van Meel and Op de Beeck, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Van Meel and Op de Beeck, 2020)

claim: Crijns et al. tested the temporal contiguity hypothesis in adult rat primary visual cortex and found that the tolerance in orientation selectivity across spatial frequency was not affected by temporal continuity manipulation.
source: Crijns et al. tested the temporal contiguity hypothesis in adult rat primary visual cortex and found that the tolerance in orientation selectivity across spatial frequency was not affected by temporal continuity manipulation (Crijns et al., 2019), which may be caused by a different representation mechanism in lower levels of visual hierarchy.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Crijns et al., 2019)

claim: Matteucci and Zoccolan reported that reduced temporal continuity experience in early postnatal life led to a loss of complex cell functional properties in rat V1.
source: On the other hand, Matteucci and Zoccolan reported that reduced temporal continuity experience in early postnatal life led to a loss of complex cell functional properties in rat V1 (Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020)

claim: Multi-electrode array recordings from two awake macaque monkeys provided 168 multi-unit IT neural sites to 64 objects for modeling use.
source: Multi-electrode array (Utah arrays) recordings from two awake macaque monkeys provided 168 multi-unit IT neural sites to 64 objects (5460 high-variation naturalistic images) for modeling use.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data source

claim: The 64 exemplar objects come from eight categories (animals, boats, cars, chairs, faces, fruits, planes, and tables).
source: The 64 exemplar objects come from eight categories (animals, boats, cars, chairs, faces, fruits, planes, and tables).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: The plasticity rate of 0.0016 nru corresponds to a firing rate change of ~0.035 spk/s per exposure event.
source: Therefore, 0.0016 nru corresponds to a FR change of ~0.035 spk/s per exposure event, which means that ~30 exposure events of this kind would give rise to 1 spk/s change in P vs. N selectivity.
evidence: Based on calculation from model parameters and IT population statistics
